```{r setup, include=FALSE}
script <- if (file.exists("R/run_project.R")) {
  "R/run_project.R"
} else {
  "blog/posts/post2/R/run_project.R"
}
source(script)
analysis <- post2_result$analysis
d <- analysis$data
sources <- post2_result$sources
get_row <- function(id) d[d$id == id, ]
ds <- get_row("data-scientists")
ec <- get_row("economists")
op <- get_row("operations-research-analysts")
ma <- get_row("management-analysts")
mr <- get_row("market-research-analysts")
fa <- get_row("financial-analysts")
money <- function(x) scales::dollar(x, accuracy = 1)
count <- function(x) scales::comma(x, accuracy = 1)
period <- paste0(ds$projection_start, "-", ds$projection_end)
post_dir <- dirname(dirname(normalizePath(script, winslash = "/")))
if (ds$growth_pct != max(d$growth_pct) ||
    ec$median_pay_usd != max(d$median_pay_usd) ||
    ma$annual_openings != max(d$annual_openings) ||
    ma$experience == "None" ||
    !setequal(d$id[d$priority_screen],
              c("data-scientists", "operations-research-analysts"))) {
  stop("The inputs change the findings. Review the article before publishing.")
}
```

An economics student opens a job site. Should the first saved search be “economist,” “financial analyst,” or “data scientist”? Familiar titles offer little guidance about where to spend application time. **Which occupations are useful starting points when a student wants good pay, growing employment, and no typical requirement for related work experience?**

I use R's `rvest` package to extract six selected [Bureau of Labor Statistics occupational profiles](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/). Their pay and employment projections can narrow a search. They cannot identify the job an economics graduate is most likely to obtain.

## Compare jobs, not academic backgrounds

A financial analyst can have an economics degree and call themselves an economist. BLS classifies jobs by work performed, rather than academic background. Here, “economists” means SOC 19-3011; the financial-analysts profile combines 13-2051 and 13-2054. The code checks that no component code appears in two comparison rows.

These are distinct occupational classifications, not exclusive groups of economics-trained people. I compare profiles separately, keep the financial aggregate labeled, and do not add their openings into a total for economics graduates. The [classification rules](https://www.bls.gov/soc/2018/soc_2018_class_prin_cod_guide.pdf) and README document the distinction.

## Fast growth does not mean the most openings

Data scientists lead projected growth at **`r ds$growth_pct`%**, compared with **`r ec$growth_pct`%** for economists over `r period`. Their median annual pay is `r money(ds$median_pay_usd)`, versus economists' `r money(ec$median_pay_usd)`. Data science therefore deserves a closer look from a student interested in quantitative work.

```{r growth-chart, fig.cap="Projected employment growth. Teal highlights profiles passing the stated preference screen, not an official BLS rating.", fig.alt="Bars compare projected growth for six BLS occupational profiles. Data scientists lead, followed by operations research analysts. Teal marks the two profiles meeting the article's pay, growth and experience preferences.", fig.width=9, fig.height=4.8}
analysis$growth_plot
```

The second chart changes the ranking. Management analysts have about `r count(ma$annual_openings)` projected openings annually, market research analysts `r count(mr$annual_openings)`, and data scientists `r count(ds$annual_openings)`. Economists have `r count(ec$annual_openings)`.

Growth measures expansion relative to an occupation's size. Openings also include replacement needs when workers retire or leave an occupation. A large, slower-growing field can therefore offer more openings than a small, fast-growing one. These are projections for all qualifying workers, not current vacancies or positions reserved for new graduates.

```{r openings-chart, fig.cap="Projected average annual openings, including replacement needs and all experience levels.", fig.alt="Bars show management analysts with the most projected annual openings and economists with the fewest. Data scientists grow fastest but have fewer projected openings than management or market research analysts.", fig.width=9, fig.height=4.8}
analysis$openings_plot
```

Taken together, the charts show why a single ranking is a poor search strategy. Searching only by growth would emphasize data science; searching only by openings would emphasize management analysis. For a new graduate, the second choice also raises an experience question. The practical task is to find a manageable set of searches consistent with the student's constraints, rather than declare one occupation universally superior.

## Turn the comparison into a search

Suppose a student chooses three preferences: median pay of at least **$85,000**, projected growth of at least **10%**, and no typical requirement for related work experience. This screen selects **data scientists and operations research analysts**. Operations research offers `r money(op$median_pay_usd)` median pay, `r op$growth_pct`% growth, and about `r count(op$annual_openings)` annual openings.

```{r comparison-table}
knitr::kable(analysis$comparison_table,
  caption = paste0("Selected BLS profiles. Pay: May ", ds$pay_year,
    "; projections: ", period, ". Financial analysts combine two SOC codes."))
```

Create saved searches in those two areas, then inspect each posting's tasks and qualifications. Both have bachelor's-level entry education in BLS, but an economics degree alone need not supply every required technical skill. Management analysis has more openings but typically requires related experience; new graduates should look specifically for campus or entry-level programs.

The recommendation depends on those preferences. Financial analysis misses the growth cutoff despite `r money(fa$median_pay_usd)` median pay. Raising the pay floor to $90,000 or growth floor to 15% leaves only data science. The code saves nine alternative screens so readers can inspect that sensitivity.

The screen is deliberately easy to change. A student willing to accept slower employment growth might retain financial analysis; one with relevant experience might investigate management analysis. Neither adjustment requires treating a national median as an expected personal offer.

## Takeaway

**Use occupational evidence to choose searches, then actual job descriptions to choose applications.** Under these preferences, data science and operations research are starting points, rather than a ranking of the best careers for every graduate. Median pay is not a starting salary, and national projections cannot reveal local competition, work-authorization requirements, or an individual's hiring probability.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Sources and reproducibility

The six public BLS Summary HTML fragments were captured September 20, 2026. Pay refers to May `r ds$pay_year`; projections cover `r period`. `rvest` extracts the Quick Facts table and annual-openings paragraph. Cleaning removes formatting; checks validate fields, measurement years, archived-file hashes and SOC coverage. Classification metadata is stored separately from scraped numbers.

```{r source-links, results='asis'}
for (i in seq_len(nrow(sources))) {
  cat(sprintf("- [%s](%s)\n", sources$occupation[i], sources$url[i]))
}
```

Rendering reads saved HTML. Optional live collection checks robots rules, spaces requests, and stops on access errors without bypassing restrictions. The [README and code](https://github.com/augenstern118/testrepo/tree/main/blog/posts/post2) document replication and all saved outputs.
:::
